readingInstruction: Read Judges 13:1-14:20. The reading introduces Samson, the most famous and the most troubling of the judges. As you read, notice how the story starts with a promising birth and a faithful couple, and slowly turns into a man ruled by his appetites. Keep in mind that his strength is a gift of the Spirit and not of his muscles.
settingTheScene: Israel has done evil again, and this time the oppressor is the Philistines, who will remain a threat until the time of David. There is a significant difference from the earlier cycles. This time, Israel does not cry out to the LORD. The text does not mention any repentance. God acts on his own initiative. He sends the angel of the LORD to a barren woman in the tribe of Dan, the wife of Manoah, and announces the birth of a son who will begin to save Israel. The stories of Samson open with a miracle birth, but they will end in blindness and death. Samson is a figure of tragic gift: a man consecrated to God from the womb who lives like everyone else.
observation: “The people of Israel again did what was evil in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD gave them into the hand of the Philistines forty years” (13:1).
The angel of the LORD appears to Manoah’s barren wife and says she will conceive a son who will be a Nazirite “from the womb” (13:3-5).
The boy is to have no razor on his head and not to drink wine, and he “shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines” (13:5).
Manoah prays for the angel to return, and the angel ascends in the flame of the altar (13:8-20).
Manoah says, “We shall surely die, for we have seen God,” and his wife reasons that if the LORD wanted to kill them, he would not have accepted their offering (13:22-23).
“The boy grew, and the LORD blessed him. And the Spirit of the LORD began to stir him” (13:24-25).
Samson demands a Philistine wife: “Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes” (14:3).
The text says that this “was from the LORD, for he was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines” (14:4).
Samson kills a lion with his bare hands, poses a riddle, and loses his wedding bet through his wife’s betrayal (14:5-20).
interpretation:
The opening chapter is one of the most beautiful in the book. A barren woman, like Sarah, Rebekah, and Rachel, is visited by God. Like Hannah later and Elizabeth after her, she will bear a child through divine intervention. The pattern is familiar: God overcomes human inability to bring salvation. The angel’s instructions emphasize that the boy is to be set apart from birth. The Nazirite vow, described in Numbers 6, included abstaining from wine, avoiding contact with the dead, and leaving the hair uncut. It was a visible sign of consecration.

Notice the contrast between Manoah and his wife. Manoah is fearful and cautious. His wife is perceptive and calm. When the angel ascends in the fire, Manoah despairs. His wife reasons from God’s character: if he intended to destroy us, he would not have accepted our sacrifice or told us these things. Her theology is sound, and it is a model of how to reason from the grace of God. She understands that God’s gifts are signs of his favor.

Then Samson grows up, and the Spirit begins to stir him, but the next scene is troubling. He sees a Philistine woman and demands, “Get her for me, for she is right in my eyes.” This phrase is the key to the whole book. “Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.” Samson is the embodiment of the age. The man consecrated to God is governed by what he sees. His parents object, and the text tells us they did not know that this was from the LORD, who was seeking an opportunity against the Philistines. This is a paradox: God uses Samson’s sin to accomplish his purposes. It does not excuse Samson. It shows that God’s plans are not thwarted by human weakness.

The lion episode reveals the source of his power: “the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon him.” His strength is not physical. It is a gift. Yet he does not tell his parents about the lion or the honey in its carcass, a hint that he has already violated his Nazirite vow by touching a carcass. His riddle at the wedding feast is built on a secret he cannot share, and he loses it to his wife’s tears. The story is a catalog of the ways a man can squander a gift.

Samson is a tragic figure, but he also points forward. His miraculous birth, his consecration, and his role as a deliverer anticipate Christ. But he is a shadow, not the substance. Where Samson indulged his appetites, Jesus resisted the tempter in the wilderness. Where Samson was blinded, Jesus gives sight to the blind. Where Samson finally pulled down a temple in death, Jesus’s death tore the veil of the temple and set people free.
connection: The Nazirite vow is described in Numbers 6:1-21. The barren-mother pattern appears in Genesis 18, 25, 29, 1 Samuel 1, and Luke 1. The angel of the LORD who ascends in fire recalls Genesis 16 and Exodus 3. The Spirit rushing upon Samson is echoed in Judges 3:10, 6:34, and 11:29, and in 1 Samuel 10:6. Hebrews 11:32 includes Samson. Jesus’s birth, consecration, and victory over Satan contrast with Samson’s failures (Luke 1-4).
application:
First, let Manoah’s wife teach you to reason from God’s grace. When you are afraid, ask what God has already done. His gifts and promises are signs of his intention to bless.

Second, examine what is “right in your eyes.” Samson’s downfall began with what he saw. What do you look at, and what do you pursue because it looks good? Bring your desires before the Lord and ask for his wisdom.

Third, remember that your gifts are not your own. Samson’s strength came from the Spirit. Whatever abilities you have, thank God for them and use them for his purposes.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for gifts you did not earn.
Ask him to keep you from living by what is right in your own eyes.
Ask him for faithfulness in your calling.
